analysis.one_liner: Adds hearings, cost tests, and easier court challenges that make it much harder for federal agencies to issue new regulations.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee for two years, never got a vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the federal rulemaking process that agencies use to write regulations. It would require agencies to pick the cheapest option that meets a statute's goals, hold courtroom-style hearings with cross-examination for rules costing $1 billion or more, and make it easier for regulated companies to challenge rules in court by letting judges second-guess agency evidence and cost estimates. The upshot would be fewer, slower, and weaker federal rules on workplace safety, pollution, food and drug safety, and consumer protection.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies facing expensive federal rules gain new tools to delay, weaken, or kill them: they could petition for hearings, cross-examine agency experts, and sue under easier standards. Businesses that rely on informal agency guidance would get clearer limits on it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large regulated businesses facing costly rules

how_it_helps.text: Agencies would generally have to adopt the least costly rule that meets statutory objectives, and justify any costlier choice on public health, safety, or welfare grounds [S3].

Rules projected to cost $1 billion or more would require an on-the-record hearing with cross-examination of the agency's evidence, and parties could petition for hearings and challenge evidence under the Information Quality Act [S3].

Courts could immediately review interim rules issued without full procedures, and judges would be barred from deferring to agency interpretations, cost-benefit analyses, or guidance that did not follow the bill's procedures [S3].

Major rules would require advance notice at least 90 days before a proposal, with at least 60 days for comment, and agencies would have to document alternatives including taking no federal action at all [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people, through weaker or slower enforcement of rules that limit pollution, unsafe workplaces, risky products, and unfair financial practices. The costs of a cheap-but-inadequate rule show up as health, safety, and environmental harm rather than as compliance expenses for industry.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone relying on federal safety rules

drawbacks.text: The default to the least costly workable rule cuts against statutes that deliberately put public health and safety ahead of compliance expense, so agencies could be pushed toward weaker standards [S3].

Requiring trial-like hearings with cross-examination for the largest rules, plus expanded and immediate judicial review, would add years of delay and litigation to rulemaking, during which unregulated hazards persist [S3].

A genuine objection the bill answers: agencies do issue costly rules on thin evidence and use informal guidance documents that function like binding rules without public process, and the bill would force documented reasoning and limits on that guidance [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some procedural improvements are real — documented evidence, longer comment periods, and limits on informal guidance would make rulemaking more transparent. But the core design tilts the whole process toward cost: the least-costly-rule default, cross-examination hearings, and judge-by-judge reweighing of agency evidence would make it systematically harder to regulate, even where the case for protection is strong. The bill trades concrete safeguards for procedural friction that falls hardest on the public.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee referred it to a subcommittee on day three and then took no further action, so it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Bob Goodlatte introduced the bill on January 3, 2017, the first day of the 115th Congress, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1] [S5].
On January 5, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law, which is the last action in its history [S5].
No markup, vote, or report ever followed; the bill remained in committee until the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].
The bill attracted only five cosponsors — four Republicans and one Democrat [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people came out ahead: agencies keep the current rulemaking process, so existing and future workplace, environmental, and consumer protections were not saddled with the bill's least-cost default and hearing requirements. Regulated industries did not get the new hearing, petition, and litigation tools the bill would have handed them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who rely on federal protections

sides.party_line_note: No floor or committee vote ever occurred; the only partisan signal is that four of the five cosponsors were Republicans, with one Democrat.

industries.industry: Regulated industries broadly (energy, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, manufacturing, finance)
industries.note: The bill would have given these companies hearings with cross-examination, a cheapest-option default for agencies, and easier court challenges to contest costly rules. Its gain comes at the cost of weaker public health, safety, and environmental protections, but the bill died in committee so the gains never materialized.

The bill would have stripped agencies of discretion to weigh benefits beyond cost, exposed their evidence to cross-examination and judicial second-guessing, and subjected their guidance to new limits. Their loss would have been the public's loss.

industries.industry: Litigation and consulting firms serving regulated companies
industries.note: Expanded judicial review, evidence petitions, and on-the-record hearings would have created years of new proceedings that regulated companies pay firms to litigate and navigate.
